title: The empire of Aksum
takeaway: Aksum grew great by sitting where trade routes met, and it faded when the routes moved. Position is power only while the traffic lasts.

scenes.say: In the highlands of what is now northern Ethiopia and Eritrea, a kingdom rose that traded with Rome, Arabia and India.
In the third century the Persian prophet Mani is said to have named four great kingdoms of the world. Aksum was one of them.

items: Cloth, wine and metal coming in
The Red Sea port of Adulis
scenes.say: Its wealth came through the port of Adulis on the Red Sea, where African goods met ships from the Mediterranean and the Indian Ocean.
Aksum struck its own gold coins from around the year 270. In the fourth century King Ezana adopted Christianity, and his coins began to carry the cross.

scenes.label: metres of carved granite, still standing
scenes.say: Its kings raised stone towers called stelae, each cut from a single block. One that still stands is about twenty-four metres tall.

scenes.words: The roads moved. The city stayed.
scenes.say: From the seventh century, Red Sea trade passed into other hands and Aksum's power drained away. Its church and its script lived on in Ethiopia.

title: How the Roman West fell
takeaway: Rome did not fall in a day. It was divided, invaded and hollowed out over two centuries, and half of it carried on for a thousand years more.

scenes.say: People speak of the fall of Rome as one event. It was closer to a slow unravelling, and only half the empire went.
In 285 Diocletian divided the empire to make it governable. In 410 a Gothic army sacked the city of Rome. In 476 the last western emperor was removed.

scenes.label: years since a foreign enemy had last taken the city
scenes.say: When the Goths entered Rome in 410, no foreign enemy had taken the city in about eight hundred years. The shock was felt across the Mediterranean.
Historians still argue about the causes. Most lists include civil war, a debased currency, armies recruited from outside, and constant pressure on the borders.

scenes.words: 476 in the West. 1453 in the East.
scenes.say: The eastern half, ruled from Constantinople, kept calling itself Roman. It lasted until 1453, almost a thousand years after the West.

title: The Council of Nicaea
takeaway: At Nicaea the church put into fixed words what it believed about Christ: that the Son is fully God, of one being with the Father.

scenes.say: In the year 325, bishops from across the Roman world met in the town of Nicaea to settle a question about who Jesus is.

scenes.words: Was the Son created, or eternal?
scenes.say: A priest from Alexandria named Arius taught that the Son of God was made by the Father and so had a beginning. Many bishops said this could not be right.

scenes.label: bishops, by the traditional count
scenes.say: The emperor Constantine called the council. Tradition gives the number of bishops as three hundred and eighteen. Modern estimates are somewhat lower.

scenes.words: Of one being with the Father.
scenes.say: The council answered with a creed. It declared the Son to be true God from true God, begotten and not made, of one being with the Father.
The argument went on for decades, and Athanasius of Alexandria spent much of his life defending the decision. In 381 a second council expanded the creed into the form recited today.

title: The printing press
takeaway: Gutenberg made copying cheap, and cheap copies meant an idea could outrun anyone trying to stop it.

scenes.say: Around 1450, in the German city of Mainz, Johannes Gutenberg began printing with movable metal type.
He was not the first to use movable type. Bi Sheng made clay type in China in the eleventh century, and a Korean book was printed from metal type in 1377.

items: Oil-based ink that held to it
scenes.say: What Gutenberg added was a system: a mould for casting letters fast, an ink that stuck to metal, and a screw press to make the impression.

scenes.label: copies of the Gutenberg Bible, roughly
scenes.say: His great Bible was finished around 1455. About a hundred and eighty copies were made, in a fraction of the time a scribe would need for one.

scenes.words: One monk's theses. All of Germany. A few weeks.
scenes.say: In 1517 Martin Luther's ninety-five theses were printed and reprinted, and within weeks they were being read across Germany.

title: Compound interest
takeaway: Growth that earns its own growth starts slowly and ends steeply. Most of the reward goes to whoever started earliest and waited longest.

scenes.say: Compound interest is interest that earns interest. It sounds like a small thing, and over decades it is not.
Put a thousand dollars away at seven percent. After a year you have a thousand and seventy. Next year you earn seven percent on all of it, not just the first thousand.
Leave it alone and the line bends upward. Ten years nearly doubles it. Forty years turns one thousand into almost fifteen thousand.
Take the interest out each year and after forty years you have three thousand eight hundred in total. Leave it in and you have almost four times that.

scenes.label: years to double at 7%, by the rule of 72
scenes.say: A quick way to estimate: divide seventy-two by the rate. At seven percent, money doubles in a little over ten years.
The same arithmetic runs against you on a loan or a card balance. What you owe grows on itself until it is paid.

title: Tenochtitlan, the city on a lake
takeaway: The Mexica turned a swampy island into one of the largest cities on earth by building with the water instead of against it.

scenes.say: Mexico City stands on the remains of another capital, one that was built on an island in the middle of a lake.
By tradition the Mexica founded Tenochtitlan in 1325 on an island in Lake Texcoco. Less than two hundred years later it ruled an empire.
Causeways tied the island to the mainland. An aqueduct carried fresh water from Chapultepec. Canoes moved goods along canals through the city.
Food grew on chinampas: beds of mud and plants raised from the shallow lake bed. They could be harvested several times a year.

scenes.label: people, by a common estimate, in 1519
scenes.say: When the Spaniards arrived in 1519, perhaps two hundred thousand people lived there. Few cities in Europe were as large.
In 1521, after a long siege, the city fell to Hernán Cortés and his many indigenous allies. Mexico City was built over its ruins.

title: How the Bible came into English
takeaway: The English Bible exists because people judged that ordinary readers should have Scripture in their own language, and some of them paid for it with their lives.

scenes.say: For most of the Middle Ages, the Bible in England was read in Latin. Putting it into English took more than two hundred years.
In the 1380s John Wycliffe and his followers translated it from Latin and copied it by hand. In 1526 William Tyndale's New Testament came off a printing press.

scenes.words: From the Greek. In print. Small enough to hide.
scenes.say: Tyndale worked from the Greek, not the Latin, and his books were printed abroad and smuggled into England in bales of cloth.

scenes.label: the year Tyndale was executed
scenes.say: The translation was banned, and Tyndale was hunted. He was arrested near Brussels and executed in 1536.
Within a few years English Bibles were being printed with royal approval. When the King James Version appeared in 1611, a large share of its New Testament was Tyndale's phrasing.

title: The 80/20 pattern
takeaway: A small share of causes usually produces most of the result. Find that share before spreading effort evenly.

scenes.say: In many situations a few causes account for most of the effect. It has a name: the Pareto principle.
In 1896 the Italian economist Vilfredo Pareto noted that about eighty percent of Italy's land belonged to about twenty percent of its people.

scenes.words: The vital few. The useful many.
scenes.say: Decades later the engineer Joseph Juran saw the same shape in factory defects: a few causes produced most of the faults. He named the idea after Pareto.

items: A few customers bring most of the revenue
A few bugs cause most of the crashes
A few habits produce most of the progress
scenes.say: The pattern shows up widely. A handful of customers, bugs or habits tend to carry most of the weight.

scenes.words: It is a pattern, not a law.
scenes.say: The numbers are rarely exactly eighty and twenty, and they need not add to a hundred. The point is the imbalance, and the question it raises: which few matter most?
